summary: I-JSON (Internet JSON) is a restricted profile of JSON designed to maximize interoperability and increase confidence that software can process it successfully with predictable results. It is meant to be used by protocols that want JSON to behave the same way everywhere.

plainLanguage.summary: I-JSON is a restricted form of JSON for Internet protocols. It limits character encodings, numbers, and object members so different software is more likely to interpret a message the same way.

questions: how is i-json different from json
how should i-json encode large integers
subtitle: A restricted form of JSON that helps different software interpret the same message consistently.

tldr.problem: JSON permits some character encodings, numeric values, and object structures that software may handle differently, causing interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: I-JSON adds rules to JSON: messages use UTF-8, exclude surrogate and noncharacter code points, avoid numbers beyond common precision, and do not repeat object member names.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can reject messages that violate the profile instead of interpreting ambiguous data. The RFC also recommends practices for protocol designers, including how to handle unknown members, dates, and binary data.

sections.title: Why Define I-JSON
sections.content:
JSON is widely used in Internet protocols, but some allowed language idioms and text encodings can lead to interoperability problems or software breakage. These problems can arise when receiving software maps JSON automatically into programming-language structures or database records.

I-JSON, short for Internet JSON, is a profile of JSON with additional constraints. Every I-JSON message is also a JSON text as defined by RFC 7159. The added rules enforce practices intended to make messages more predictable.
sections.plainLanguage: I-JSON adds limits to JSON so programs are less likely to disagree about the meaning of a message. An I-JSON message is still JSON, but it must follow these extra rules.

sections.title: Encoding and Allowed Characters
sections.content:
An I-JSON message MUST use UTF-8 encoding. Object member names and string values MUST NOT contain Unicode code points that identify Surrogates or Noncharacters.

This restriction applies whether a character appears directly in the UTF-8 text or as an escape sequence. The RFC gives � as an invalid unpaired surrogate, while 𐊭 is permitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Every I-JSON message must use UTF-8. Names and text values cannot include Unicode surrogate or noncharacter code points, whether written directly or as escapes.

sections.title: Numbers and Exact Values
sections.content:
I-JSON senders SHOULD NOT include numbers with greater magnitude or precision than an IEEE 754-2008 binary64 (double-precision) number provides. A sender cannot expect a receiver to treat an integer as exact if its absolute value exceeds 9007199254740991.

When an application needs exact interchange of numbers beyond these limits, the RFC RECOMMENDS encoding them as JSON strings. The receiving program must understand the string's intended meaning. The RFC gives 64-bit integers as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs may not preserve very large or very precise JSON numbers exactly. If exact values beyond the supported number range are needed, send them as strings and define how the receiver should read them.

sections.title: Object Member Names
sections.content:
An I-JSON object MUST NOT contain duplicate member names. Two names are duplicates when, after escape sequences are processed, they contain the same sequence of Unicode characters.

Object member order does not change the meaning of an I-JSON message. A receiver MAY treat two messages as equivalent when their only difference is the order of object members.
sections.plainLanguage: An object cannot use the same name for two members, even if one name uses escaped characters. Changing the order of members does not change the message's meaning.

sections.title: How Receivers Handle Messages
sections.content:
Receivers can reject or disregard messages that do not meet the I-JSON requirements. A protocol using I-JSON can require its receivers to reject nonconforming messages or, for security protocols, to avoid trusting them.

Protocol designers SHOULD provide a way for the receiver to report an error to the sender when it receives invalid data.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver can reject a message that breaks the I-JSON rules instead of guessing what it means. Protocol designers should also give receivers a way to report the problem.

sections.title: Recommendations for Protocol Designers
sections.content:
I-JSON messages may contain any JSON value at the top level. However, some older software accepts only a JSON object or array at the top level, so protocol designers SHOULD avoid other top-level values when they want maximum interoperability.

The RFC recommends a Must-Ignore policy: software MUST NOT treat an unrecognized protocol element as an error, and should process the rest of the transaction as if the element were absent. It also RECOMMENDS representing timestamps and durations as strings using RFC 3339 with uppercase letters, an explicit time zone, and trailing seconds even when they are 00. Arbitrary binary data is RECOMMENDED to be placed in a string using base64url encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: For compatibility, place a JSON object or array at the top level and have software ignore members it does not recognize. The RFC also recommends a consistent string format for times and base64url strings for binary data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations that apply to JSON in RFC 7159 also apply to I-JSON. The RFC identifies no additional security considerations specific to I-JSON.

Because I-JSON forbids some JSON practices that can cause unpredictable behavior in receiving software, the RFC says it may provide a more secure basis for Internet protocols and may suit protocol designers with special security needs.
sections.plainLanguage: I-JSON does not remove the security concerns that apply to JSON. Its stricter rules may reduce unpredictable interpretations, but protocol designers still need to address JSON security risks.

items.title: Top-level value
items.text: Prefer an object or array for compatibility with older software.

items.title: Unknown members
items.text: Ignore protocol elements that the implementation does not recognize.

items.title: Time and date
items.text: Use strings following the RFC's RFC 3339-based recommendations.

items.title: Binary data
items.text: Use a string encoded with base64url.
